title: Senior's toolkit: processes, services and logs
summary: systemctl, journalctl, drop-ins, timers, ps, top, vmstat, the OOM killer and lsof for an on-call shift.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: processes, services and logs
steps.body: When a service misbehaves, these answer: is it running, what did it say, what is it using, and did the kernel kill it.

toolkit.what: State, main PID, recent exit codes and the last log lines of a service, all in one screen.
flags: print everything, do not cut long lines
restart, or ask it to re-read config
start now and at every boot

toolkit.what: The service's logs from the journal, filtered by time, priority or text.
Creates a drop-in override instead of editing the packaged unit file, so upgrades do not undo your change. It reloads systemd for you.
flags: show the unit plus all drop-ins
needed after editing unit files by hand

toolkit.what: systemd timers, the modern replacement for cron: when each job last ran and when it runs next.
flags: catch up on runs missed while the machine was off

toolkit.what: Every process with the columns you choose, sorted. `pgrep -af` finds processes by command line.
Live load. In `top`, press `P` (CPU), `M` (memory), `1` (each CPU), `c` (full command). `vmstat 1` prints one line a second: run queue, swap, IO wait.
flags: memory, including what the page cache can give back

toolkit.what: Kernel messages with readable times. The OOM killer logs here when it kills the biggest process to save the machine.
flags: the same through the journal, with `--since`
toolkit.example: sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'out of memory|killed process'

toolkit.what: Lists open files: which process holds a port, a file, or a deleted file that still uses disk space.
flags: open files that were deleted (space not yet freed)

steps.prompt: `orders-api` restarts every few hours. `systemctl status` shows `Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL`, and the app's own log has no error at all. What do you check first?
options: `dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'out of memory|killed process'` (or `journalctl -k`): the kernel OOM killer
Add more logging to the app
steps.explain: SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the app cannot log it. When nobody sent it by hand, the OOM killer is the usual sender, and it writes the victim, its memory and the time to the kernel log.

steps.prompt: `/` is 100% full. You deleted a 20 GB `app.log`, but `df -h` still says 100%. What do you run?
options: `sudo lsof +L1`: the app still has the deleted file open; restart it (or truncate through `/proc/<pid>/fd`)
steps.explain: Deleting removes the name, but the space is freed only when the last process closes the file. Next time, empty the file with `truncate -s 0 app.log` instead of deleting it, and set up log rotation.

steps.prompt: Follow the service's logs, starting from one hour ago.
steps.explain: `-u` picks the unit, `--since` sets the start, `-f` follows. `-k` would show kernel messages and `--until` sets the end.

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
pairs: start it now and at every boot
add an override that survives package upgrades
show the unit file and every drop-in
see when scheduled jobs run next

steps.prompt: A service is down. Put the triage in order.
lines: Fix the cause the logs point to

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Start every service problem with `systemctl status` and `journalctl -u --since`; check `dmesg -T` whenever you see `signal=KILL`. Change units only with `systemctl edit`, and prefer a timer to a crontab line so the job's runs and logs live in the journal.
